title: Walking Calories by Distance: Kcal Estimates
description: Estimate calories burned over a walking distance with Walking Calories by Distance — weight-based, clearly approximate. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, under the simple model this page uses, a 160 lb walker covers a mile at roughly 56 kcal — so a 5-mile walk is about 280 kcal, before hills comment.
quick_answer: Walking Calories by Distance estimates the energy a walk costs from the walker's weight and the distance covered. Enter both and read an approximate kilocalorie figure — a planning estimate built on a simple, stated model that leaves out hills, pace and terrain, and says so on the page.

popular_table.intro: Estimates at an explicitly stated assumption of roughly 0.35 kcal per pound of body weight per mile — a planning model, not a measurement. Faster and hillier walking burns more.
popular_table.note: Your watch's figure and this model's will differ; consistency in your own tracking beats agreement between models.

faq: Does this replace a specialist tool or professional measurement?
No — it is a weight-and-distance estimate with its assumption printed. Wearables with heart-rate data estimate closer; a lab measures. This is the planning figure.
Is my input uploaded?
No. Weight and distance are used in your browser and go nowhere.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Traffic does not burn the walker's calories; hills do, and the model omits them — treat the output as a floor.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
You burn calories over the ground you actually walk. Enter the walked distance.
Can route results change over time?
Your weight and fitness do; the model stays fixed so your log stays comparable across the change.
Why does weight matter so much?
Walking is carrying: energy scales with the mass moved over the distance. The model is linear for the same reason the physics is.
Net or gross calories?
The model estimates the walk's energy cost as a planning figure. Net-versus-gross bookkeeping is a dietitian's refinement beyond a distance model.
Why do step counters disagree with the model?
They count motion; the model prices distance and weight. Two honest instruments, two questions — a log should pick one ruler.
Walking with a backpack?
Add the pack to the carried weight in spirit: energy follows total mass moved. The model takes body weight; your judgement adds the rucksack.
Downhill walks burn less?
Yes — gravity assists. The flat model overstates a descent day and understates the climb back. Net days average out honestly.
